I try hard to control my emotions

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank

issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind' implies a fragmented, snapshot-like recollection, whereas 'My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed' implies a broadly coherent and detailed memory. That pair is difficult to reconcile as describing the same trauma memory without qualification, making the memory profile internally inconsistent. 'Partial Clarity' could fit with either style, but the simultaneous endorsement of both strongly snapshot-like and globally vivid/detailed memory is the main coherence problem.

vignette: Maya Vance had been twenty-eight when her boyfriend’s younger brother, Eli, collapsed on the floor of the taproom where she poured drinks. The trauma did not arrive as a narrative; it arrived as a sequence of sharp, unblinking frames. She remembers the exact angle of his fall, the sickening thud against the oak bar top, and the way his shoes scraped uselessly against the polished floorboards. For an hour, Eli lay completely still while she pressed her apron to his mouth, her fingers slick with his blood, waiting for sirens that seemed to take forever. When he finally passed on the way to the hospital, Maya’s mind locked onto the most graphic moments while leaving the intervening hours completely blank. Those fragmented, photographic flashes do not fade; instead, they sharpen her negative outlook on the world. Because she is certain her own hesitation during those first minutes cost him precious seconds, she has come to believe the event happened because of the way she acted. That heavy self-blame, paired with a growing suspicion that her coworkers and family only offered empty reassurances, actively narrows her recall. Rather than allowing her mind to process the loss, her distrust forces her memory to fixate relentlessly on the worst visual details, while the gaps in her recall remain untouched by comfort or context. The specific potency of her triggers stems from that unscripted collapse; the taproom’s familiar neon signs now promise the same sudden medical emergency, making every crowded shift feel like a walking liability. The sudden, unblinking images that flood her mind make it impossible to tolerate ordinary stimulation. When she sees a headline about a sudden collapse or a friend mentions a nearby overdose, the visceral pictures of Eli’s stiffening body take over, so she has quietly deleted every local news app and avoided any medical settings that might trigger a similar panic. This withdrawal is compounded by a rigid need to manage her internal state. Because she believes she failed him and can't rely on others, she has built a wall of rigid emotional control around herself, refusing to let her voice crack or her hands shake in public. She will sit in her beat-up Honda for twenty minutes after closing just to ensure her face is perfectly neutral before she walks through her boyfriend’s door. By denying herself the comfort of shared grief and steering completely clear of psychological support, she inadvertently starves her own coping mechanisms. The silence she maintains convinces her that reaching out is fundamentally futile, which in turn tightens her grip on self-blame and deepens her distrust of everyone around her. Over the past decade, this self-reinforcing loop has frayed her daily life. Her boyfriend notices how she flinches when he mentions a hospital, and she has grown exhausted at work, constantly scanning the taproom for any sign of a patron stumbling while bracing for another catastrophe. Her PCL5 score of thirty-eight reflects the heavy toll of these habits, but it is her partner’s quiet plea last week that finally broke through her resistance. He found her lying on the bathroom floor, not from a medical crisis, but from sheer emotional depletion, and gently placed a card for a trauma therapist on the sink. Maya is terrified that opening up to a stranger might force her to confront the blank spaces in her memory, but she is also desperately hoping that someone might finally tell her it was not entirely her fault.
